analysis.one_liner: Bans lead in toys and other products made for children under six.
analysis.headline: The Lead Free Toys Act was introduced with 10 Senate sponsors, was referred to the Commerce Committee the same day, and never received a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill orders the Consumer Product Safety Commission to write rules classifying any product marketed to children under 6 that contains more than trace amounts of lead as a banned hazardous substance, taking those products off the market [S2] [S3]. If the Commission decides some electronic devices cannot comply right away, it must set standards to reduce lead exposure in them and a deadline for full compliance [S2] [S3]. The bill was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee the day it was introduced and never moved again [S1] [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Children under 6 and their parents, who would no longer face toys, jewelry, and other children's products containing more than trace amounts of lead, a metal that harms brain development. The Commission's ban would cover anything marketed for or foreseeably used by children under 6 [S2] [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Children under six and their parents

how_it_helps.text: Directs the Consumer Product Safety Commission, within 180 days of enactment, to issue regulations classifying any children's product containing more than trace lead as a banned hazardous substance, meaning it could no longer legally be sold [S2] [S3].
Covers not just toys but any consumer product marketed for use by children under 6, or whose substantial use by them is foreseeable — a broader net than a toy-only rule [S3].

Closes the usual escape hatch for electronics: if some devices cannot comply immediately, the Commission must still issue lead-reduction standards for them and put them on a mandatory schedule to reach full compliance [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Toy and children's product makers, and electronics manufacturers, who would have to reformulate or withdraw products containing lead and absorb testing and compliance costs; some of those costs would likely be passed to consumers in prices [S2] [S3].

drawbacks.text: The bill gives the Commission no new money and sets a 180-day deadline to write regulations defining 'trace amounts' of lead for entire categories of children's products — a rush that invites weak or hasty standards [S2] [S3].
Reformulating products and testing for lead costs manufacturers money, especially smaller toymakers, and some costs would likely show up in prices [S3].

The electronics carve-out means devices deemed infeasible to fix would keep containing lead for some time, only subject to 'reduce exposure' standards until their compliance deadline arrives [S2] [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit — removing lead, a proven neurotoxin, from products used by children under 6 — is large and one-sided; the costs are ordinary compliance and reformulation expenses that product-safety rules routinely impose, softened for electronics by a phased schedule. The main design weakness is the unfunded 180-day rulemaking deadline, which could pressure the Commission into loose definitions. On balance the bill's benefits clearly outweigh its costs.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never took it up, and it died when the 110th Congress ended in January 2009.

narrative.text: Senator Obama introduced the bill on May 3, 2007, joined by Senators Durbin and Clinton; it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation the same day [S3] [S5].
Nine other senators cosponsored it — 8 Democrats and 1 Independent [S4].
The action history shows nothing after the referral: no committee hearing, no markup, no floor vote. The bill sat in committee until the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009 [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Toy and electronics makers were better off because the bill never moved — they faced no lead ban from this bill. Children and parents got nothing from it.

for.name: Sen. Barack Obama
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and steered it to the Senate Commerce Committee

for.name: Sens. Dick Durbin and Hillary Clinton
for.what_they_did: Joined Obama in introducing the bill on day one

against.name: Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on May 3, 2007 and never held a hearing, markup, or vote on it; the action history records no committee activity at all [S5]

against.name: Sen. Daniel Inouye
against.role: Chairman, Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee
against.what_they_did: As chairman, never scheduled the bill for committee consideration; the record shows no action after referral

sides.party_line_note: All 10 sponsors were Democrats or an Independent and no Republican signed on, but the bill never got a vote, so no one ever had to go on record for or against it [S3] [S4].

industries.note: The bill would have banned selling any product for children under 6 containing more than trace lead, forcing reformulation or withdrawal of affected products [S2] [S3]. Their cost is the point: lead in children's products is exactly what the bill exists to remove.

Devices the Commission deemed infeasible to fix would get lead-reduction standards and a compliance schedule instead of an immediate ban — a softer landing, but an eventual deadline to get lead out [S2] [S3].
A ban on children's products containing lead would remove those items from store shelves, and retailers would bear the cost of pulling inventory and verifying compliance [S3].
